stories.headline: Capcom confirms breach of over 11.7 million CAPCOM ID accounts
stories.in_brief: Capcom disclosed that a third‑party intrusion exposed email addresses and account activity data for more than 11.7 million users, and passwords on 196 accounts were changed without authorization. The company says services remain online and urges users to watch for phishing attempts.
stories.so_what: The breach affects a large portion of Capcom's global player base, exposing personal identifiers such as email addresses, account creation dates, last‑login timestamps and IP addresses. While credit‑card data and most passwords appear untouched, the unauthorized password changes on 196 accounts demonstrate that attackers had valid credentials, raising the risk of credential‑stuffing and targeted phishing campaigns. Capcom has reset the altered passwords, set up regional support channels, and claims to have addressed the attack method, but it has not disclosed technical details. Users should remain vigilant for fraudulent communications that reference the breach, as the stolen data can be used to craft convincing scams. Observers will watch for any further disclosures about the intrusion vector and whether additional accounts are compromised.
stories.what_to_do: 1. Enable two‑factor authentication on your CAPCOM ID account. 2. Review your account details and linked platform accounts for any unauthorized changes. 3. Treat any email claiming to be from Capcom with suspicion; verify by visiting cid.capcom.com directly and avoid clicking links or opening attachments.

claims.quote: In an alert today, the gaming company says that passwords for all other registered members have not been exposed and that credit card information remained unaffected.

stories.headline: China-linked Storm-0940 leverages AI tool ARTEX in ConnectWise supply chain breach
stories.in_brief: Microsoft says the state‑aligned group Storm-0940 used the AI penetration‑testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks on the ConnectWise Cloud Backup service. The campaign targeted thousands of tenants worldwide, accelerating credential abuse and privilege escalation.
stories.so_what: The use of an AI‑driven tool marks a shift in how nation‑state actors conduct supply‑chain attacks, allowing them to scan, spray passwords and abuse OAuth applications at machine speed. By automating reconnaissance and credential‑spraying, the threat actor reduced the window for detection to minutes, with some privileged access achieved in under three hours. Organizations using ConnectWise services, especially those with integrated Microsoft 365 environments, should anticipate faster, larger‑scale intrusion attempts and reassess their detection and response capabilities. Watch for further disclosures from Microsoft on remediation guidance and for any indicators of compromise related to the ARTEX framework or the Quad7 botnet.
stories.what_to_do: 1. Apply any available patches or updates to ConnectWise Cloud Backup. 2. Review and tighten OAuth application permissions in Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. 3. Enable multi‑factor authentication and monitor for abnormal sign‑in patterns, especially rapid failed login bursts.

stories.headline: First Human Death Linked to Shamonda Virus Reported in France
stories.in_brief: A man in his sixties with severe immunosuppression died on 9 October after becoming the first known person infected with the Shamonda virus. Health authorities say the case is exceptional and the risk to the public remains low.
stories.so_what: The confirmed human infection marks the first documented case of a virus previously thought to affect only livestock. Researchers note that the patient likely contracted the virus from a biting midge, a common vector for orthobunyaviruses that circulate among cattle and other animals. While no human‑to‑human transmission has been recorded for orthobunyaviruses, the incident highlights the potential for zoonotic spillover, especially among immunocompromised individuals. Public health agencies in several European countries are monitoring the situation, but both French officials and the French government assert that there is no immediate risk to the general population. Ongoing investigations aim to confirm the transmission route and assess whether broader surveillance or preventive measures, such as insect control, are needed as the virus spreads in European livestock.

stories.so_what: The penalty stems from a data‑privacy lawsuit tied to Meta’s 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal. The case also reflects ongoing tension between state regulators and large technology companies over data‑privacy accountability. Meta’s chief legal officer has said the company will appeal, so the final financial impact remains uncertain. Observers will watch appellate courts for precedent‑setting decisions that could affect future state‑level enforcement actions against tech firms nationwide.

stories.headline: Hubble captures gravitational lens to aid upcoming Roman telescope studies
stories.in_brief: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope photographed a foreground galaxy 4.5 billion light‑years away lensing a background galaxy 8 billion light‑years distant. The image demonstrates how Hubble’s detail and Roman’s wide‑field infrared will together probe galaxy mass and dark matter.
stories.so_what: The Hubble image provides a concrete example of the synergy between the aging observatory and the soon‑to‑launch Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. By resolving the arc‑counterarc lens configuration, scientists can measure how much mass—including invisible dark matter—lies in the foreground galaxy. These measurements will calibrate Roman’s broader surveys, improving estimates of dark‑matter distribution across the universe. As Roman begins operations, similar lensing observations will expand from case studies to statistical samples, refining cosmological models and informing theories of galaxy formation. Observers should watch for Roman’s first data releases later this decade, which will build on the techniques demonstrated by Hubble today.

stories.headline: AI‑generated Pink Panther images misrepresented as France protest footage
stories.in_brief: Viral posts claimed a person in a Pink Panther costume was taking part in the October 2026 French protests. Fact‑checkers found the images and videos were created with artificial‑intelligence tools and repurposed older photos.
stories.so_what: The false Pink Panther content spread widely on social media, giving the impression of a whimsical yet confrontational mascot amid civil unrest in France. By identifying invisible SynthID watermarks and other AI signatures, researchers showed the material was fabricated using Google, OpenAI and Meta tools. Reverse‑image searches linked the visuals to unrelated protests in Armenia (2015), Greece (2010) and Kenya (2025), demonstrating how AI can recycle historic footage to fabricate current events. This case highlights the growing risk that AI‑generated media can be weaponised to distort public perception of political demonstrations, potentially inflaming tensions or undermining trust in legitimate reporting. Monitoring tools and transparent verification processes will be essential as similar deep‑fake claims emerge in future protests worldwide.
stories.what_to_do: Check for AI watermarks, use reverse‑image search, and consult reputable fact‑checkers before sharing viral protest media.
